Indira Gandhi: During her father Jawaharlal Nehru's premiership from 1947 to 1964, Gandhi was his hostess and accompanied him on his numerous foreign trips.

Louis XIV (Louis-Dieudonné; 5 September 1638 – 1 September 1715) was King of France from 14 May 1643 until his death in 1715.

Bundestag: The Bundestag (German: [ˈbʊndəstaːk], 'Federal Diet') is the federal parliament of Germany.

Mahsa Amini protests: Iran. At least 551 people, including 68 minors, had been killed as a result of the government's intervention in the protests, as of 15 September 2023.
In which country did the Battle of Leipzig take place?
Battle of Leipzig: Kingdom of Saxony. The Battle of Leipzig, also known as the Battle of the Nations, was fought from 16 to 19 October 1813 at Leipzig, Saxony.
In which country did the Battle of Tours take place?
Battle of Tours: France. Details of the battle, including the number of combatants and its exact location, are unclear from the surviving sources.
In which country did the Battle of Plassey take place?
Battle of Plassey: India. The battle helped the British East India Company take complete control of Bengal in 1773.

2016 Nice truck attack: France. The driver was Mohamed Lahouaiej-Bouhlel, a Tunisian living in France.

Bahmani Kingdom: India. The Bahmani Kingdom, or the Bahmani Sultanate, was a late medieval Persianate kingdom that ruled the Deccan Plateau in India.

Central Park jogger case: United States. On the night Meili was attacked, dozens of teenagers had entered the park, and there were reports of muggings and physical assaults.

Shimabara Rebellion: Japan. The Shimabara Domain was given to Kōriki Tadafusa.

Operation Linda Nchi: Somalia. Operation Linda Nchi (Swahili: Linda Nchi; "Protect the Country") was the Kenya Defence Forces' invasion of southern Somalia beginning in 2011.
Which of these was an official language of Papal States?
Papal States: Latin. At their zenith, the Papal States covered most of the modern Italian regions of Lazio (which includes Rome), Marche, Umbria, Romagna, and portions of Emilia.
Which of these was an official language of the Yemen Arab Republic?
Yemen Arab Republic: Arabic. The Yemen Arab Republic was formed in 1962, when a coup in the capital Sana'a saw Nasserist military officers overthrow the monarchy and proclaim a republic.
Which of these was an official language of the Tuvan People's Republic?
Tuvan People's Republic: Mongolian. The Tuvan People's Republic (TPR), known simply as Tuva, was a partially recognized socialist republic that existed between 1921 and 1944 in North Asia.
Which country used the Spanish real as its official currency?
The Spanish real is the official currency of Crown of Castile. In 1492, the voyage of Christopher Columbus and the discovery of the Americas were major events in the history of Castile.
Responsible for the 1998 US embassy bombings, the USS Cole attack, and the September 11 attacks, this pan-Islamist militant organization sought a global caliphate — name it?

Al-Qaeda is a pan-Islamist militant organization led by Sunni Islamist jihadists who self-identify as a vanguard spearheading a global Islamist revolution to unite the Muslim world under a supra-national Islamic caliphate.
A Bolshevik who served from Lenin through Stalin and Khrushchev all the way to Brezhnev, this Soviet survivor inspired the saying "from Ilyich to Ilyich" — which statesman was he?
Anastas Mikoyan was Soviet statesman and revolutionary (1895–1978).
This former bureaucrat turned anti-corruption activist won a Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2006, then became the 7th Chief Minister of Delhi — who is he?
Arvind Kejriwal (Hindi; born 16 August 1968) is an Indian politician, activist and former bureaucrat, who served as the 7th Chief Minister of Delhi.
In 751, an Abbasid-Tibetan force defeated Tang China's army for control of territory near the Syr Darya, ending Tang expansion into Central Asia — which clash?
Battle of Talas (pinyin: Dlus Zhny) was an armed confrontation between the Abbasid Caliphate along with the Tibetan Empire against the Tang dynasty and its allies in 751.
Guided by ten principles like radical inclusion and radical self-reliance, this week-long event climaxes with the torching of a giant wooden effigy in Nevada's Black Rock Desert — what is it?
Burning Man is a week-long large-scale desert event focused on "community, art, self-expression, and self-reliance" held annually in the Western United States.
Fill in the blank: “____ refers to a December 2008 assault that took place in Ansan, South Korea.”

Cho Doo-soon case refers to a December 2008 assault that took place in Ansan, South Korea. An eight-year-old girl known by the pseudonym Na-young (나영) was kidnapped and raped by Cho Doo-soon, a 56-year-old male, in a bathroom inside a church.
Born among the Tugen of the Rift Valley and once a schoolteacher, which man became Kenya's longest-serving president, ruling from 1978 to 2002?
Daniel arap Moi (2 September 1924 - 4 February 2020) was a Kenyan politician who served as the second president of Kenya from 1978 to 2002.
Led by expelled ANC youth leader Julius Malema since 2013, this Marxist, Pan-Africanist party won 25 seats in its first South African election — which party?
Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) is a South African communist and black nationalist political party.
According to Abrahamic tradition, this was the first woman created by God, whose name means 'living one' or 'source of life.' Who is she?
Eve is a figure from the Book of Genesis in the Old Testament.
The third woman ever elected to Congress from Arizona, this politician left office in 2012 after a severe brain injury from an assassination attempt — who is she?
Gabby Giffords (born June 8, 1970) is an American retired politician and gun violence prevention advocate.

This American politician has served as the 48th Governor of Texas since 2015, after stints as state attorney general and a justice on the Texas Supreme Court, making him the nation's longest-serving incumbent governor — who is he?
Greg Abbott (born November 13, 1957) is an American politician, attorney, and jurist who has served since 2015 as the 48th governor of Texas.
This German chancellor's 16-year tenure — the longest in the country's post-war history — spanned the end of the Cold War, German reunification, and the founding of the European Union — who is he?
Helmut Kohl (3 April 1930 - 16 June 2017) was a German politician who served as chancellor of Germany and governed the Federal Republic from 1982 to 1998.
This Venezuelan leader renamed his country the "Bolivarian Republic" and gave his name to a whole political ideology before dying in office in 2013 — who was he?
Hugo Chávez (28 July 1954 - 5 March 2013) was a Venezuelan politician, revolutionary, and military officer who was the president of Venezuela from 1999 until his death in 2013.
The eldest son of a former U.S. president and first lady, this businessman and environmentalist ran as the Democratic nominee in Nevada's 2006 Senate election — who is he?
Jack Carter (politician) (born July 3, 1947) is an American businessman, politician and environmentalist.
Before becoming U.S. secretary of defense in 2017, this Marine Corps four-star general led both U.S. Central Command and NATO's Supreme Allied Command Transformation — who is he?
Jim Mattis (born September 8, 1950) is an American military officer who served as the 26th United States secretary of defense from 2017 to 2019.
A mountain range on Pluto and an asteroid both bear her name — fitting for the Japanese climber who was the first woman atop Everest and the first to bag the Seven Summits. Who was she?
Junko Tabei (ne Ishibashi; 22 September 1939 - 20 October 2016) was a Japanese mountaineer, author and teacher.
Carved out of a former Electorate after Napoleon dissolved the Holy Roman Empire in 1806, this southern German monarchy lasted until 1918 — which one?
Kingdom of Württemberg was a German state that existed from 1806 to 1918, occupying territory in what is now the southern German federal state of Baden-Wrttemberg.

Born from the anti-authoritarian faction that split from the Marxists within the International Workingmen's Association, this political tradition champions workers' self-management while rejecting the state — what is it called?
Libertarian socialism is an anti-authoritarian and anti-capitalist political current that emphasises self-governance and workers' self-management.

A Chinese revolutionary and political theorist who founded the People's Republic of China in 1949, he adapted Marxism to the Chinese context in a theory now known by his name. Who led from 1949 until his death in 1976?
Mao Zedong (26 December 1893 - 9 September 1976) was a Chinese revolutionary, politician, writer, political theorist and the founder of the People's Republic of China (PRC).
Named after a 16th-century Frisian cleric who was a contemporary of Martin Luther, these Anabaptist Christian communities trace their roots to the Radical Reformation — who are they?
Mennonites are a group of Anabaptist Christian communities tracing their roots to the epoch of the Radical Reformation.

In Hindu tradition it's the highest of life's four aims — above dharma, artha, and kama — and across Jainism, Buddhism, and Sikhism it names liberation from the cycle of death and rebirth. What is it?
Moksha (UK also), also called vimoksha, vimukti, and mukti, is a term in Jainism, Buddhism, Hinduism, and Sikhism for various forms of emancipation, liberation, nirvana, or release.

A general of the Army of the Republic of Vietnam, this man led South Vietnam from 1964 to 1965 — bouncing between head of state and prime minister — before exile sent him to die in San Jose. Who is he?
Nguyễn Khánh (8 November 1927 - 11 January 2013) was a Vietnamese military officer and politician.
This giant huntsman of Greek myth was placed among the stars by Zeus or Artemis, and one legend even credits him with carving out the shape of the Strait of Sicily — who is he?
Orion (mythology) (: Ancient) was a giant huntsman whom Zeus or Artemis placed among the stars as a constellation.
A member of Vietnam's Politburo since 2016 and once the Party Secretary of Quảng Ninh province, this politician became his country's eighth prime minister in 2021 — who is he?
Phạm Minh Chính (born 10 December 1958) is a Vietnamese politician and former public security lieutenant general.

Succeeding the pharaoh who had stabilized Egypt at the end of the 18th Dynasty, this short-reigned ruler founded the 19th Dynasty and was father to one of ancient Egypt's most storied pharaohs — who is he?

Ramesses I was the founding pharaoh of ancient Egypt's 19th Dynasty. The dates for his short reign are not completely known but the timeline of late 1292–1290 BC is frequently cited as well as 1295–1294 BC.

Arguing that cheaper letters would mean more letters and thus higher profits, this English teacher and reformer championed a Uniform Penny Post and is credited with inventing the postage stamp — who was he?
Rowland Hill (3 December 1795 - 27 August 1879) was an English teacher, inventor and social reformer.

Drafted into the Imperial Russian Army as a cavalryman before joining the Red Army in 1917, this Ukrainian-born officer went on to become one of World War II's most prominent Soviet commanders — who is he?
Semyon Timoshenko was Soviet military commander (1895–1970).

A Cypriot barrister who founded his own Democratic Party, he took office as president after Makarios III's death in 1977 and greatly expanded his island nation's presence on the world stage. Who was he?
Spyros Kyprianou (28 October 1932 - 12 March 2002) was a Cypriot barrister and politician, who served as President of Cyprus from 1977 to 1988.
Landing at Anzac Cove in 1915 and later helping plan the Battle of Pozières, this soldier rose to become the only Australian ever to reach the rank of field marshal. Who was he?
Thomas Blamey (24 January 1884 - 27 May 1951) was an Australian general of the First and Second World Wars.
This businessman-turned-politician became Mexico's first president in over 70 years not drawn from the long-ruling PRI, winning the 2000 election with 43 percent of the vote — who was he?
Vicente Fox (Latin American; born 2 July 1942) is a Mexican businessman and politician who served as the 62nd president of Mexico from 2000 to 2006.
This Ohioan holds a singular distinction: he is the only person to have served as both U.S. president and chief justice of the United States. Who was he?
William Howard Taft (September 15, 1857 - March 8, 1930) was the 27th president of the United States from 1909 to 1913 and the tenth chief justice of the United States from 1921 to 1930.
A trained electrical engineer who dared to criticize Mao's economic policies in 1957 and got branded a 'rightist' for it, this man later served as China's premier from 1998 to 2003 — who is he?
Zhu Rongji (born 23 October 1928) is a Chinese retired politician and electrical engineer who served as the 5th premier of China from 1998 to 2003.

Alauddin Khalji: Sultan of Delhi from 1296 to 1316. Alauddin Khalji (Persian: علاء الدین خلجی; born Ali Gurshasp; c. 1266 – 4 January 1316) was the Khalji dynasty Sultan of Delhi from 1296 until his death in 1316.
Known to local tribespeople as the 'hero of the jungle,' this Indian revolutionary led a 1922 guerrilla rebellion against British rule in the Andhra-Odisha borderlands — who is he?
Alluri Sitarama Raju: Indian freedom fighter and revolutionary.
Serving as Governor of Jakarta before running for president in 2024, this Indonesian politician founded a program that sends university graduates to teach for a year nationwide — who is he?

A close aide to Egyptian presidents Nasser and Sadat, this official was allegedly a Mossad spy who fed Israel intelligence before the Yom Kippur War, then died mysteriously falling from a London balcony in 2007 — who was he?
Ashraf Marwan: Egyptian businessman and spy (1944–2007)
This Indian engineer-turned-politician served as Karnataka's 17th chief minister from 2021 to 2023 before becoming a Lok Sabha MP for Haveri — who is he?
Basavaraj Bommai: 23rd Chief Minister of Karnataka from 2021 to 2023. In July 2022, Bommai became only the second person from BJP to complete one year as chief minister of the state.

Lasting three days in September 2004, this hostage crisis in North Ossetia, Russia, took over 1,100 captives including 777 children and is considered history's deadliest attack on an educational institution — which crisis?
Beslan school siege: 2004 Russian hostage crisis and massacre.
Lasting from 1858 to 1947, this era of Crown rule over the Indian subcontinent blended directly governed provinces with princely states under British paramountcy. What was it?
British Raj: 1858–1947 Crown colonial rule in India.

Identified chiefly by a shared family of Indo-European languages, this collection of ancient peoples included the Gauls, the Britons and Picts of Britain and Ireland, and the Galatians of Anatolia — who were they?
Celts: Collection of indo-European peoples sharing Celtic languages and cultural practices.
The Gospels present Jesus as the Son of God and say his coming as the messiah had already been prophesied. In which part of the Bible was that prophecy said to appear?

Christianity is an Abrahamic monotheistic religion based on the Bible and the teachings of Jesus. The Gospels state that Jesus is the Son of God and rose from the dead after his crucifixion, and that his coming as the messiah was prophesied in the Old Testament and chronicled in the New Testament.
This philosophical idea holds that all humans belong to a single community and should live as 'world citizens' guided by universal moral standards — what is it called?
Cosmopolitanism: Idea that all human beings are members of a single community.
A former co-owner of Talenti Gelato and Belvedere Vodka, this Minnesota congressman became the first Democrat to win his district in sixty years — who is he?
Dean Phillips: American businessman and politician (born 1969)

Doug Burgum: American politician and businessman (born 1956)
The second of Islam's two main festivals, the Feast of the Sacrifice, falls on the 10th day of which month?
Eid al-Adha, the Feast of the Sacrifice, is the second of the two main festivals in Islam alongside Eid al-Fitr. It falls on the 10th of Dhu al-Hijjah.
An early ally of Hitler, he co-founded and led the Nazi Party's brownshirt paramilitary, the SA — until the SS assassinated him in 1934 during the Night of the Long Knives. Who was he?
Ernst Röhm: German Nazi military officer (1887–1934)
Founded in 1926 by Éamon de Valera after a split from Sinn Féin, which party has been one of Ireland's two dominant political forces ever since?
Fianna Fáil: Irish political party. The party dominated Irish political life for most of the 20th century, and, since its foundation, either it or Fine Gael has led every government.
Emerging from a wave of 1848 revolutions that toppled the monarchy, this government lasted only four years before an emperor's proclamation ended it in 1852. What was it called?

French Second Republic: Government of France from 1848 to 1852. The republic existed from 1848, when the monarchy fell, until its dissolution only four years later in 1852 upon the proclamation of the Second French Empire.

George Wallace: American politician and lawyer (1919–1998)

This 10th-century king introduced Christianity to Denmark and united Jutland and Zealand under his rule, before being ousted by his own son — who was he?

Harald Bluetooth: 10th-century King of Denmark and Norway. Harald "Bluetooth" Gormsson (Old Norse: Haraldr Blátǫnn Gormsson; Danish: Harald Blåtand Gormsen, died c. 985/86) was a king of Denmark and Norway.
Also known as the White Huns, this Central Asian people defeated the Kidarites in 450 CE before falling to a joint Turkic-Sasanian force in 560 — who were they?
Hephthalites: 5th–8th-century nomadic confederation in Central Asia.

This cadet branch of the Capetian line ruled France from 1328 to 1589, spinning off junior branches in Orléans, Anjou, Burgundy, and Alençon before its male line died out and the Bourbons took over — which royal dynasty?
House of Valois: Cadet branch of the Capetian dynasty. The Capetian House of Valois (VAL-wah, also US: va(h)l-WAH, French: [valwa]) was a cadet branch of the Capetian dynasty.
A locksmith's apprentice turned committed communist, this Hungarian politician led the 1956 uprising against the Soviet-backed government — and was executed for it two years later. Who was he?
Imre Nagy: Hungarian politician and leader of the 1956 revolution (1896–1958)
Ruling Kuwait from 1977 until his death in 2006, this emir led the country through the Gulf War against Saddam Hussein's Iraq with US backing — who is he?
Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah: Emir of Kuwait from 1977 to 2006. The 13th ruler in his family's dynasty, Jaber's reign oversaw the transition of a relatively traditional society into a modernized state.
Leader of La France Insoumise, this French politician has run for president three times and announced a fourth bid for 2027 — who is he?
His eleven years in the top job make him Australia's second-longest-serving prime minister, trailing only Robert Menzies — which member of parliament for Bennelong led the country from 1996 to 2007?
John Howard: Prime Minister of Australia from 1996 to 2007. Howard was born in Sydney and studied law at the University of Sydney.

Charles I of Spain awarded this navigator a coat of arms reading "Primus circumdedisti me" — "You were the first to circumnavigate me" — after he completed the first voyage around the Earth aboard the Victoria. Who was he?
Juan Sebastián Elcano: Spanish seafarer and circumnavigator.
Symbolized by the Six Arrows, this political ideology stemmed from the sweeping secularizing reforms of Turkey's founding president — which ideology is it?
Kemalism: Founding ideology of the Republic of Türkiye.
A towering figure whose political career spanned seven decades, this Greek statesman served four terms as prime minister and two as president of the Third Hellenic Republic — who was he?
The 17th king of Sparta's Agiad dynasty, which claimed descent from Heracles, he led the allied Greek last stand at Thermopylae against the Persians; who was he?
Leonidas I: King of Sparta from c. 489 BC to 480 BC.

Crowned King of France just before his ninth birthday after his father Henry IV was assassinated, this monarch later seized power by exiling his own mother and executing her favorite, Concino Concini — who was he?
Louis XIII: King of France from 1610 to 1643.

Because British insurers wouldn't pay claims tied to a "civil war," colonial officials coined a euphemistic name for this 1948-1960 guerrilla conflict against communist independence fighters — which conflict?
Malayan Emergency: 1948–1960 British colonial war in Malaya. The communists gained support from many civilians, mainly those from the Chinese community.
Serving as Bavaria's Minister-President since 2018, this German politician has also led the region's dominant conservative party since 2019 — who is he?
A former physician, she became First Lady of Azerbaijan and, in 2017, was appointed by her husband the president to a newly created role as First Vice President — who is she?
Mehriban Aliyeva: First Vice President of Azerbaijan since 2017.
Described in the Hebrew Bible as the older sister of Moses and Aaron, this prophetess led the Israelite women out of Egypt and taught them Torah — who is she?
Miriam: Sister of Moses and Aaron. The Torah refers to her as "Miriam the Prophetess" and the Talmud names her as one of the seven major female prophets of Israel.
Nicknamed 'Netaji' by his party, this Indian politician founded the Samajwadi Party and served three terms as Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh — who is he?
Launched in 2017 by Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman, this Saudi megaproject at the northern tip of the Red Sea was eventually scaled way back amid delays, cost overruns, and criticism — what is it?
Neom: Planned city in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Fulfilling a prophecy despite his father's attempt to thwart it, which mythical king of Thebes unwittingly killed his father and married his mother?
Oedipus: Mythical Greek king of Thebes. Oedipus (UK:, also US:; Ancient Greek: Οἰδίπους Oidípous, lit. 'swollen foot') was a mythical Greek king of Thebes.

Established in the 8th century when the Frankish king Pepin the Short granted land to the pope, this Italian sovereign territory was ruled directly by the Church until Italian unification in 1870 — what was it?
Papal States: Italian state ruled by the pope (756–1870)
A close ally of Robespierre, this French revolutionary chose suicide over arrest when authorities stormed the Hôtel de Ville during the coup of 9–10 Thermidor — who was he?
Published in 2023 by the Heritage Foundation, which initiative pairs a 'Mandate for Leadership' policy document with a loyalist-staffing database to consolidate executive power?
Project 2025: Conservative political initiative in the United States.
Founded in 1997 by Lalu Prasad Yadav, this Bihar-based political party built its support among Other Backward Classes, Dalits, and Muslims — which party?
Rashtriya Janata Dal: Political party in India. The Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD, lit. 'National People's Party') is an Indian political party, mainly based in the Indian state of Bihar.
This former Navy SEAL took part in the 2011 raid that killed Osama bin Laden and later stirred controversy by claiming he alone fired the fatal shot — who is he?
Robert J. O'Neill: US Navy SEAL (born 1976)
Born in London to a Pakistani family, this Labour politician served as MP for Tooting before becoming the third mayor of London in 2016?
Sadiq Khan: Mayor of London since 2016. Sir Sadiq Aman Khan (born 8 October 1970) is a British politician serving as the third and current strategic authority mayor for London since 2016.
These horse-mounted nomads swept out of Central Asia to dominate the Pontic Steppe by the 8th century BC, later raiding West Asia after crossing the Caucasus — who were they?
Scythians: Nomadic Iranic people of the Pontic Steppe.
One of Noah's sons in Genesis, this biblical figure is considered an ancestor of Abraham and lent his name to the term for a group of West Asian peoples — who is he?
Shem: Biblical figure, son of Noah. Shem (Hebrew: שֵׁם Šēm; Arabic: سَام, romanized: Sām) is one of the sons of Noah in the Bible (Genesis 5–11 and 1 Chronicles 1:4).
The first pharaoh of Egypt's Fourth Dynasty pioneered new pyramid-building techniques, leaving at least three pyramids still standing today — who was he?
A physician trained in Hong Kong, he turned revolutionary after the Qing government rejected his 1894 reform petition, and went on to found the Republic of China and the Kuomintang. Who is he?
Sun Yat-sen: Chinese revolutionary and statesman (1866–1925)
Serving as deputy president under Nelson Mandela before succeeding him as South Africa's president in 1999, he later resigned in 2008 at his party's request — who is he?
Thabo Mbeki: President of South Africa from 1999 to 2008. As president, Mbeki had an apparent predilection for foreign policy and particularly for multilateralism.
A vocal champion of the crypto industry in Congress, this Minnesota Republican has served as House majority whip since 2023 after narrowly losing a gubernatorial bid in 2010. Who is he?
Symbolizing both a diamond's indestructibility and a thunderbolt's force, this ritual scepter-like tool is used alongside a bell in Tibetan Buddhist ceremonies — what is it called?
Vajra: Spiritual weapon or symbol in Dharmic religions.
A key figure of Chile's Nueva Canción movement, this singer-songwriter was arrested and killed in the days following the 1973 coup that overthrew President Allende — who was he?
Víctor Jara: Chilean folk singer and activist (1932–1973)
The only person ever to lead both branches, this Skull and Bones member from Cincinnati served as the 27th U.S. president and later as Chief Justice of the United States — who is it?
William Howard Taft: President of the United States from 1909 to 1913.

Rooted in pre-Islamic Kurdish tradition and shaped by Sufi influence, this monotheistic faith reveres a 'Peacock Angel' as chief among seven angels tasked with guarding the world — which religion is it?
Nicknamed 'The Acquitator' for his string of courtroom wins as a criminal defense lawyer, he served as France's Minister of Justice from 2020 to 2024 — who is he?
Éric Dupond-Moretti: French-Italian politician and lawyer (born 1961)
Which one below was born first?
Joseph Schumpeter (born 1883) is the earliest of the four. Joseph Alois Schumpeter (German: [ˈʃʊmpeːtɐ]; February 8, 1883 – January 8, 1950) was an Austrian political economist.
Who among these was born first?
Patrick Geddes (born 1854) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these was founded earliest?
Bash (Unix shell) (founded 1989) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was established earliest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is a physicist?
Which of these is a chemist?
Ellen Swallow Richards is a chemist. Richards graduated from Westford Academy (second oldest secondary school in Massachusetts) in 1862.
What is the atomic number of Moscovium?
Moscovium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Mc and atomic number 115.
What is the atomic number of Bismuth?
Bismuth is a chemical element; it has symbol Bi and atomic number 83.
In what year did Marie Curie die?
Marie Curie: Curie was born in Warsaw, Russian Empire, where she studied at the clandestine Flying University and began her practical scientific training.
In what year was Sodium discovered?
Sodium is a chemical element; it has symbol Na (from Neo-Latin natrium) and atomic number 11.
Ammonium chloride: Pfizer. Ammonium chloride is an inorganic chemical compound with the chemical formula NH4Cl, also written as [NH4]Cl.
Boeing 777X: United States. The Boeing 777X is an American long-range, wide-body, twin-engine airliner built by Boeing Commercial Airplanes, undergoing flight testing.
Who is credited with discovering Telescopium?
Telescopium: Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Its name is a Latinized form of the Greek word for telescope.
Who is credited with discovering Spontaneous generation?
Spontaneous generation: Anaximander. It was hypothesized that certain forms, such as fleas, could arise from inanimate matter such as dust, or that maggots could arise from dead flesh.
Who is credited with discovering SN 1987A?
SN 1987A: Ian Shelton. SN 1987A was a Type II supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.
This Onmyōdō master advised Heian emperors on astrology and spiritual matters; a Kyoto shrine and an Osaka train station now honor him — who is he?
Abe no Seimei (February 21, 921 AD - October 31, 1005) was a Japanese onmyji, a court official and specialist of Onmyd, during the middle of the Heian period.
First approved in the United States in 1966, this xanthine oxidase inhibitor treats high uric acid levels linked to gout, kidney stones, and chemotherapy — what medication is it?
Allopurinol is a medication used to decrease high blood uric acid levels.
Nicknamed 'the heart of the scorpion,' this distinctly reddish variable star is the brightest in the constellation Scorpius — what is it?
Antares is the brightest star in the constellation of Scorpius. It has the Bayer designation α Scorpii, which is Latinised to Alpha Scorpii.

Named for the Ancient Greek word for 'star' after its flower shape, this group of roughly 170 mostly Eurasian perennial plants is also known for its late-blooming 'Michaelmas daisies' — which plant group?
Aster (genus) is a genus of perennial flowering plants in the family Asteraceae.
Once chairman of the Nasdaq, this financier admitted to masterminding the largest-known Ponzi scheme in history, estimated at $65 billion — who was he?

Bernie Madoff (April 29, 1938 - April 14, 2021) was an American financier, con artist, and stock broker who was the admitted mastermind of the largest-known Ponzi scheme in history, worth an estimated $65 billion.
This family of cloven-hoofed, ruminant mammals includes cattle, bison, buffalo, antelopes, sheep, and goats across 143 living species — name the family?
Bovidae is the biological family of cloven-hoofed, ruminant mammals that includes cattle, bison, buffalo, antelopes, and goat-antelopes such as sheep and goats.
Sole living family in the mammalian suborder Tylopoda, which group unites camels with llamas and their South American relatives?
Camelidae is a family of mammals belonging to the ungulate order Artiodactyla (even-toed ungulates) and the only living family in the suborder Tylopoda.
A secondarily aquatic clade within the order that also includes hippos, this infraorder covers whales, dolphins and porpoises, along with extinct relatives like Basilosaurus — which group of animals?

Cetacean are marine mammals belonging to the infraorder Cetacea, a secondarily aquatic clade under the order Artiodactyla that include whales, dolphins, porpoises and extinct groups such as Basilosaurus.

From a tree in the myrtle family, these dried flower buds from the Moluccas are harvested year-round across different countries and lend their scent to everything from cosmetics to cooking — what are they?
Clove are the aromatic flower buds of a tree in the family Myrtaceae, Syzygium aromaticum.

This naturally occurring but largely inactive steroid hormone shields organs like the kidneys from active cortisol, and gets converted back into cortisol by an enzyme mainly in the liver — what hormone is it?
Cortisone is a naturally occurring, mostly inactive pregnene (21-carbon) steroid hormone.
The word names both a noun — a plan or proposal made by a thinking agent — and a verb for developing one, always aiming to satisfy goals while weighing function and aesthetics; what is it?
Design is the concept or proposal for an object, process, or system.
This soil-dwelling invertebrate of the phylum Annelida is also known by slang names like 'dew-worm,' 'rainworm,' and 'nightcrawler.' What creature is it?
Earthworm is a soil-dwelling terrestrial invertebrate that belongs to the phylum Annelida.

A German Jew who fled the Nazi regime for the United States, this social psychologist and psychoanalyst co-founded a New York psychiatric institute and was associated with the Frankfurt School of critical theory — who is he?
Erich Fromm (March 23, 1900 - March 18, 1980) was a German-American social psychologist, psychoanalyst, sociologist, humanistic philosopher, and democratic socialist.
Bred in Brazil as a guard dog, cattle herder, and big-game hunter, this large mastiff-type breed was also once used to catch runaway slaves — which breed?
Fila Brasileiro (Portuguese) is a Brazilian breed of large working dog of mastiff type.

Cataloged by the astronomer Ptolemy in the second century AD and still one of the 88 modern constellations, this zodiac constellation takes its Latin name from the mythological twins Castor and Pollux — what's the constellation?
Gemini (constellation) is one of the constellations of the zodiac and is located in the northern celestial hemisphere.

Native to the Amazon basin, this climbing plant's coffee-bean-sized seeds can contain up to 6% caffeine — roughly double the concentration found in green coffee beans — and flavor a popular Brazilian soft drink. Name the plant?
Guarana (from the Portuguese guaran; Paullinia cupana, syns.

This colorless, nearly odorless organic compound is a straight-chain alkane with six carbon atoms, widely used as a cheap, largely unreactive solvent and found in small amounts in modern gasoline blends — what is it?
Hexane is an organic compound, a straight-chain alkane with six carbon atoms and the molecular formula C6H14.
This medical condition occurs when the body, or a region of it, is deprived of adequate oxygen at the tissue level — what is it called?

Hypoxia (medicine) is a condition in which the body or a region of the body is deprived of an adequate oxygen supply at the tissue level. Hypoxia may be classified as either generalized, affecting the whole body, or local, affecting a region of the body.

This English mathematician made foundational contributions to matrix and invariant theory, founded the American Journal of Mathematics at Johns Hopkins, and was teaching at Oxford when he died. Who was he?
James Joseph Sylvester (3 September 1814 - 15 March 1897) was an English mathematician.

The first woman of Indian origin to fly to space, this astronaut and aerospace engineer first studied in India before earning advanced degrees in the US and flying aboard Space Shuttle Columbia in 1997 — who was she?
Kalpana Chawla (July 1, 1962 - February 1, 2003) was an Indian-American astronaut and aerospace engineer who was the first woman of Indian origin to fly to space.
This small Arctic rodent is a key prey source for tundra carnivores and is the subject of a persistent myth that it marches off cliffs in mass suicide — what animal is it?
Lemming is a small rodent, usually found in or near the Arctic in tundra biomes.
Named for a Dutch physicist, this six-parameter family of linear equations converts spacetime coordinates between reference frames moving at constant relative velocity — what is it?
Lorentz transformation are a six-parameter family of linear transformations from a coordinate frame in spacetime to another frame that moves at a constant velocity relative to the former.

A student of Marie Curie, this French physicist discovered a new element in 1939 by purifying lanthanum laced with actinium, and went on to become the first woman elected to the French Académie des Sciences — who was she?
Marguerite Perey (19 October 1909 - 13 May 1975) was a French physicist and a student of Marie Curie.

This American theoretical physicist and science communicator, a professor at the City College of New York, won a 2021 lifetime achievement award named for a famous science-fiction author, honoring his work bridging science and sci-fi. Who is he?
Michio Kaku (born January 24, 1947) is an American theoretical physicist, science communicator, futurologist, and writer of popular science.
Scholars can't even agree on which elements define it, yet it appears in every human society as a vehicle for creativity through composition and performance — what is it?
Music is the arrangement of sound to create some combination of form, harmony, melody, rhythm, or otherwise expressive content.
A highly corrosive mineral compound with the formula HNO3, this strong inorganic acid is colorless but yellows over time as it decomposes. What is this acid?
Nitric acid is an inorganic compound with the formula HNO3. The compound is colorless, but samples tend to acquire a yellow cast over time due to decomposition into oxides of nitrogen.
This systemic skeletal disorder develops when the rate of bone breakdown outpaces new bone formation with age, leaving bones porous, less dense, and prone to fracture — what's the condition called?
Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disorder characterized by low bone mass, micro-architectural deterioration of bone tissue leading to more porous bone, and consequent increase in fracture risk.
Brought on by too little niacin, this disease announces itself with the 'three D's' — dermatitis on sun-exposed skin, diarrhea, and dementia — what is it?
Pellagra is a disease caused by a lack of the vitamin niacin (vitamin B3).
Which condition, more common in people with obesity or a family history, involves hair and skin debris being drawn into tissue through tiny skin openings called pits?
Pilonidal disease is a type of skin infection that typically occurs as a cyst between the cheeks of the buttocks and often at the upper end.

This corticosteroid drug treats a huge range of conditions — from rheumatoid arthritis and asthma to eye inflammation and certain cancers — and can be taken orally, injected, or applied to the skin. What is it?
Prednisolone is a corticosteroid, a steroid hormone used to treat certain types of allergies, inflammatory conditions, autoimmune disorders, and cancers, electrolyte imbalances, and skin conditions.
This root vegetable in the mustard family, whose entire plant (leaves included) is edible, was domesticated in Asia and is now grown worldwide — what vegetable is it?
Radish (Raphanus sativus or Raphanus raphanistrum subsp.
This big, sociable black corvid is told apart from its relatives by a bare, whitish patch on its face, and it nests in noisy treetop colonies near farms and villages — which bird is it?
Rook (bird) (Corvus frugilegus) is a member of the family Corvidae in the passerine order of birds.

These pinnipeds, distinguished from true seals by their external ear flaps and ability to walk on all fours, belong to the eared-seal family alongside fur seals, with six living species worldwide. What animal is this?
Sea lion are pinnipeds characterized by external ear flaps, long foreflippers, the ability to walk on all fours, short and thick hair, and a big chest and belly.

Named from an Ancient Greek word for 'soap,' this cheesy secretion of shed skin cells, oils, and moisture collects under the foreskin in males and around the folds of female genitalia — what is it called?
Smegma (from Ancient Greek, smgma, 'soap') is a cheesy substance composed of shed skin cells, skin oils, and moisture that occurs in male and female mammalian genitalia.
A Canadian cognitive psychologist at Harvard who champions evolutionary psychology and the computational theory of mind, which popular-science author wrote on how children learn irregular verb forms?
Steven Pinker (born September 18, 1954) is a Canadian cognitive psychologist, psycholinguist, popular science author, and public intellectual.
This protective cap of repetitive nucleotide sequences guards the ends of eukaryotic chromosomes from progressive degradation — what is it called?
Telomere (from Ancient Greek (tlos) 'end' and (mros) 'part') is a region of repetitive nucleotide sequences associated with specialized proteins at the ends of linear chromosomes (see Sequences).
Divided into the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis, this core section of the body is where the head, neck, and all four limbs attach — which body part?
Torso is the central part, or the core, of the body of many animals (including human beings), from which the head, neck, limbs, tail and other appendages extend.
Measuring under five feet long, this critically endangered porpoise is endemic to a small corner of Mexico's Baja California coast — which species?
Vaquita (v-; Phocoena sinus) is a species of porpoise endemic to the northern end of the Gulf of California in Baja California, Mexico.
Inspired by the code-breaking game Mastermind, this once-a-day puzzle gives you six tries and colored tiles to crack the same word everyone else is solving — which game?
The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom
Wordle is a web-based word game created and developed by the Welsh software engineer Josh Wardle.

This organic compound functions as a neurotransmitter in the brain and body of many animal types, including humans. It is the chemical that motor neurons release at the neuromuscular junction to enable muscle movement. What is it?
Acetylcholine: Organic chemical and neurotransmitter. Its name is derived from its chemical structure: it is an ester of acetic acid and choline.
Born in 1929 and died in 2001, this man was a respected Saudi Islamic scholar — who is he?

Native to South Africa's Western Cape, this flowering bulb genus lends its common name to popular winter houseplants that actually belong to a different genus, Hippeastrum — which bulb, also called the naked lady or Jersey lily?
Amaryllis: Genus of plants. Amaryllis is the only genus in the subtribe Amaryllidinae (tribe Amaryllideae).
Named from Greek words for 'curved' and 'vertebra,' this type of arthritis causes long-term inflammation where the spine meets the pelvis — what is it?
Ankylosing spondylitis: Type of arthritis of the spine. Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a type of arthritis from the disease spectrum of axial spondyloarthritis.
Known commonly as palms, this family of over 2,600 flowering plant species includes climbers, shrubs, and tree-like forms mostly found in the tropics — what's the family called?
Arecaceae: Palm family of flowering plants.
This genus of early African hominins, which lived during the Pliocene and Early Pleistocene, is considered ancestral to the genus that includes modern humans — which genus?
Australopithecus: Genus of hominin ancestral to modern humans. The genera Homo (which includes modern humans), Paranthropus, and Kenyanthropus evolved from some Australopithecus species.
Coming on over about 48 hours, this temporary facial paralysis droops one side of the face and can heighten sensitivity to sound — what condition is it?
Bell's palsy: Facial paralysis. Bell's palsy is a type of facial paralysis that results in a temporary inability to control the facial muscles on the affected side of the face.
This organ stores urine received from the kidneys via the ureters before it exits through the urethra, and gives us the medical term 'cystitis' when inflamed — what is it?
Bladder: Organ in vertebrates that collects and stores urine from the kidneys before disposal.
Typically housed in the head near the organs for vision, hearing, and smell, this organ processes thought and cognition while coordinating muscle activity — which organ?
Brain: Organ central to the nervous system.
Native to the Americas from Patagonia to western Canada, members of this succulent plant family thrive in the bone-dry Atacama Desert — what are they?
Cactus: Family of mostly succulent plants, adapted to dry environments.

A German child prodigy turned director of the Göttingen Observatory, this mathematician, astronomer, and physicist made landmark contributions across number theory, algebra, statistics, and probability — who is he?
Carl Friedrich Gauss: German polymath and scholar (1777–1855)
This Italian physician who died in 1909 is considered the founder of modern criminology, arguing that 'born criminals' could be spotted by physical defects — who is he?
This complex of DNA and histone proteins packages long strands of genetic material into compact structures while controlling access for transcription, replication and repair — what is it?
Chromatin: Complex of DNA and protein in eukaryotic cells.

Triggered by an abnormal immune response to gluten found in wheat, barley, and rye, this chronic autoimmune condition mainly affects the small intestine and often causes malabsorption in children — which condition?
Coeliac disease: Autoimmune disorder. Coeliac disease (Commonwealth English) or celiac disease (American English) is a chronic autoimmune disease, mainly affecting the small intestine.
This group of RNA viruses, named for the club-shaped spikes that crown their surface, causes illnesses ranging from the common cold to SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 — what are they called?
Coronavirus: Subfamily of viruses in the family Coronaviridae.
Inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, this disorder coats the lungs and other organs in thick mucus, inviting repeated bacterial infections — what genetic condition is it?
Cystic fibrosis: Genetic disorder affecting mostly the lungs.

Doctors once spotted this endocrine condition by its three Ps — polydipsia, polyuria, and polyphagia, or excessive thirst, urination, and hunger — all tracing back to trouble with insulin. Which disease is it?
Diabetes: Group of endocrine diseases characterized by high blood sugar levels.

Aristotle's Poetics contrasted this performance-based mode with the epic and the lyrical, and its name comes from a Greek word meaning "deed" or "act" — the two-masks symbol marks its split into comedy and tragedy. What is it?
Drama: Artwork intended for performance; formal type of literature.
Named for the large trunk-like proboscis of its males, this giant oceangoing pinniped can weigh up to 4,000 kilograms and was once hunted nearly to extinction for lamp oil. What animal is it?
Elephant seal: Genus of aquatic carnivores.
Sold under the brand name Nexium, this proton pump inhibitor treats acid reflux by blocking an enzyme in the stomach's acid-producing cells — what is it?
Esomeprazole: Medication which reduces stomach acid.
While its deciduous neighbors drop everything and go bare for winter, this kind of plant keeps its foliage green and working all year round — what's the botanical term?
Evergreen: Plant that has leaves in all seasons.

Modern phylogenetics calls this a paraphyletic group covering nearly every vertebrate except the tetrapods — gill-bearing, limbless-of-digits, and usually cold-blooded. What aquatic animals are these?
This mathematical principle links differentiation and integration, showing the two operations to be essentially inverses of each other — what is it called?
Fundamental theorem of calculus: Relationship between derivatives and integrals.
The longest member of the weasel family at up to 1.8 meters, this noisy, highly social river-dweller lives in family groups along the Amazon and in the Pantanal — which animal?
Known as the black shag in New Zealand, this widespread seabird breeds across much of the Old World, Australasia, and the Atlantic coast of North America — which bird?
This German-American physicist won a 1967 Nobel Prize for explaining how a nuclear cycle powers heavy stars, after heading the Theoretical Division at Los Alamos during World War II — who is he?
Also nicknamed 'rose mallow,' this genus of large, showy tropical flowers includes both herbaceous plants and woody shrubs — which genus is it?
Hibiscus: Genus of plants. Hibiscus is a genus of common flowering plants in the mallow family, Malvaceae.
In its pure form it's a faintly blue, syrupy liquid, but the concentrated 'high-test' version decomposes explosively when heated and has even been used as rocket fuel — what compound is it?
Hydrogen peroxide: Chemical compound. The molecule hydrogen peroxide is asymmetrical and highly polarized.

Named for the indigo-blue line seen in its spectrum when discovered in 1863, this soft, silvery-white metal with atomic number 49 is used to make the transparent conductive coating on flat-panel displays — what is it?
Indium: Chemical element with atomic number 49 (In)
Before he proposed that the Earth behaves like one self-regulating living system, this English independent scientist built the detector that first revealed CFCs lurking in our atmosphere. Who was he?

An Alberta-born clinical psychologist and University of Toronto professor, he drew huge attention in the late 2010s for his cultural and political views — self-identifying as a classical liberal. Who is he?
Often miscalled a 'bear,' this tailless, fluffy-eared Australian marsupial is actually a close cousin of the wombat — what is it?
Koala: Arboreal herbivorous marsupial native to Australia.

Native to the dry grasslands and deserts of Afghanistan, Iran, Pakistan, India, and Nepal, this ground-dwelling reptile is so widely captive-bred it's considered the first domesticated species of its kind — what is it?
Leopard gecko: Species of reptile. The leopard gecko is a popular pet, and due to extensive captive breeding it is sometimes referred to as the first domesticated species of lizard.
Based on the L-188 Electra airliner and distinguished by a tail 'stinger' used to magnetically detect submarines, this four-engine turboprop has served the US Navy since the 1960s — which aircraft?
Lockheed P-3 Orion: Maritime patrol and anti-submarine aircraft family.
Occurring naturally as the mineral brucite, this poorly soluble white solid neutralizes stomach acid in a well-known antacid — which compound?
Magnesium hydroxide: Inorganic compound of formula Mg(OH)2.
Part of the chamomile tribe within the sunflower family, some species in this plant genus share the common name 'mayweed' — which genus?
Once made by roasting wood — hence its old name 'wood alcohol' — this simplest alcohol smells much like the drinkable kind but is far more poisonous. What is it?

A hemiparasitic plant that taps into its host tree via a structure called the haustorium to steal water and nutrients, its European species was introduced to Northern California in 1900 — what plant is it?
Mistletoe: Common name for various parasitic plants.

Grouping over 30 inherited disorders that cause progressive weakening and wasting of skeletal tissue — with the Duchenne form affecting roughly half of all cases in young boys — what's this disease group called?
Muscular dystrophy: Diseases in which skeletal and visceral muscles break down over time.
A cable-like bundle of axons wrapped in three layers of connective tissue, this structure carries electrochemical signals called action potentials — what is it?
Nerve: Cable-like bundle of axons. The axons are bundled together into groups called fascicles, and each fascicle is wrapped in a layer of connective tissue called the perineurium.

This healthcare profession blends the art and science of caring, focusing on protecting and promoting health, preventing illness, and easing suffering through compassionate, hands-on care — what field is it?
Nursing: Health care profession. Nurses may help coordinate care performed by other providers or act independently as nursing professionals.
Farmed largely around a South African town, this flightless bird is the heaviest bird alive and can sprint 70 km/h — the fastest of any bird on land. What is it?
Ostrich: Genus of largest living birds.
Cultivated across the tropics for its fragrant essential oil, over 90% of this mint-family herb's global oil supply now comes from Indonesia — which plant?
Native to Eurasia but now introduced worldwide, this game bird has been flagged in the UK as a threat to endangered native adders — what is it?
Members of this eukaryotic kingdom mostly make their own food with chlorophyll, though parasitic kinds have ditched photosynthesis entirely to feed off others — what kingdom is it?
Plant: Kingdom of organisms. Historically, as in Aristotle's biology, the plant kingdom encompassed all living things that were not animals, and included algae and fungi.
This corticosteroid treats conditions from rheumatoid arthritis to asthma but can cause bone loss and psychiatric side effects with long-term use — what is it called?
Prednisolone: Corticosteroid medication. It can be taken by mouth, injected into a vein, used topically as a skin cream, or as eye drops.
Excess fluid pooling in the lungs' air sacs impairs oxygen exchange and can be triggered by either heart failure or a range of unrelated causes — what condition is this?
Pulmonary edema: Fluid accumulation in the tissue and air spaces of the lungs.
This bird of prey, related to eagles and buzzards, now breeds only in Europe but has wandered as far as Finland and the Gambia — what raptor is it?
Red kite: Species of bird. The red kite (Milvus milvus) is a bird of prey in the family Accipitridae, which also includes many other diurnal raptors such as eagles, buzzards, and harriers.
Defined by a single pair of ever-growing incisors in each jaw, this mammalian order makes up about 40 percent of all mammal species — which order?
Rodent: Order of mammals. The rodent fossil record dates back to the Paleocene of Asia.
Commonly known as elder, with its blossoms called elderflower and its fruit elderberry, this genus contains between 20 and 30 flowering plant species — which genus?

Triggered when the body's own dysregulated response to infection starts damaging its tissues and organs, this life-threatening condition brings fever, rapid heartbeat, and confusion — which condition?

Sepsis: Life-threatening response to infection. Sepsis is a potentially life-threatening condition that arises when the body's dysregulated response to infection causes injury to its own tissues and organs.
Roughly 21 feet long yet coiled to fit inside the abdomen, this digestive tube receives bile and pancreatic juice and is divided into the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum — which organ?
Small intestine: Organ in the gastrointestinal tract.
Prized as the standard soundboard material for stringed instruments, this coniferous genus has four-sided needles and dominates boreal forests across the Northern Hemisphere — which tree genus?
Spruce: Genus of coniferous evergreen trees.
This tangy reddish spice, made from a shrub in the cashew family, is a staple of Arab cuisine and holds symbolic significance on the Haft-sin table at Persian New Year — what is it?
Sumac: Related species of plants in the family Anacardiaceae.
Prized for its durability and water resistance, this tropical hardwood with a leather-like smell when freshly milled is a top choice for boat building — what is it?
Teak: Tree species native to South and Southeast Asia.
Colored metallic blue on top and silvery below for camouflage, this genus of warm-blooded ocean fish includes the giant Atlantic bluefin and eight of the true tuna species — what genus is it?
Thunnus: Genus of fishes. Thunnus is a genus of ocean-dwelling, ray-finned bony fish from the mackerel family, Scombridae.
Named for its three heads — medial, lateral, and long — which upper-arm muscle straightens the elbow when it contracts?
Triceps: Muscle on the back of the upper arm. The triceps, or triceps brachii (Latin for "three-headed muscle of the arm"), is a large muscle on the back of the upper limb of many vertebrates.
Also known by the common names bilberry, blaeberry, and whortleberry, this holarctic shrub produces edible blue fruit — what is it?
Neither bee nor ant despite being closely related, yellowjackets and hornets belong to this narrow-waisted insect group that can deliver a painful sting — what is it?
Wasp: Group of insects. Unlike true parasites, the wasp larvae eventually kill their hosts.

Denied European certification after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, this single-aisle airliner made its maiden flight from Irkutsk in 2017 and is built by a UAC subsidiary of Rostec — which aircraft?
Yakovlev MC-21: Twin-engine Russian jet airliner.
What is the chemical symbol for lithium?
The symbol for lithium is Li. Lithium is a chemical element; it has symbol Li and atomic number 3.
The symbol for helium is He. Helium is a chemical element; it has symbol He and atomic number 2.

In what year was Winona Ryder born?
Winona Ryder: Winona Laura Horowitz ( wi-NOH-nə; born October 29, 1971), known professionally as Winona Ryder, is an American actress.
In what year was Kendall Jenner born?
Kendall Jenner: Kendall Nicole Jenner (born November 3, 1995) is an American model, socialite and media personality.
In what year was Tommy Lee Jones born?
Tommy Lee Jones: Thomas Lee Jones (born September 15, 1946) is an American actor, film director, and former football player.
In what year was Val Kilmer born?
Val Kilmer: Val Edward Kilmer (December 31, 1959 – April 1, 2025) was an American actor.
In what year was Michelle Yeoh born?
Michelle Yeoh Choo Kheng (YOH;; Chinese: 楊紫瓊; born 6 August 1962) is a Malaysian actress.
In what year was Ian McShane born?
Ian McShane: Ian David McShane (born 29 September 1942) is an English actor.
In what year was Lana Rhoades born?
Lana Rhoades is an American internet personality, podcaster and former pornographic film actress.
In what year was Gwyneth Paltrow born?
